questions.prompt: Streptococcus pyogenes shows up in several virulence-factor lists. Which combination does the course attribute to it?

options.text: M-protein, kinase, and hemolysins
Coagulase, superantigens, and siderophores
Invasins, IgA protease, and LPS
Capsule, collagenase, and A-B toxin

questions.prompt: Staphylococcus aureus appears in several lists. Which combination fits it?

options.text: Invasins, LPS endotoxin, and siderophores that steal iron
Coagulase, Type I superantigen, and a leading HAI cause (MRSA)
Kinase, Type II hemolysin, and M-protein for throat adherence
IgA protease, a thick capsule, and hyaluronidase for gangrene

questions.explanation: S. aureus is coagulase-positive, makes toxic shock superantigen, and is the HAI 'problem child.'

questions.prompt: Streptococcus pneumoniae relies on which pair to avoid host defenses?

options.text: M-protein and hemolysins
Coagulase and kinase
A capsule and IgA protease
Invasins and siderophores

questions.explanation: The capsule blocks phagocytosis; IgA protease destroys mucosal antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Gram stain and toxins is FALSE?

options.text: Endotoxins are proteins secreted by Gram-positive bacteria.
LPS sits in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
Exotoxins are mostly secreted by Gram-positive bacteria.
Both superantigens and endotoxins can cause shock.
Endotoxins are released mainly when Gram-negative cells die.

questions.explanation: Endotoxins are part of the Gram-negative cell wall (LPS); exotoxins are the secreted proteins.

questions.prompt: A pathogen is carried from a pig farm's sewage into a river and makes people sick miles downstream. Map the steps.

options.text: Reservoir: pigs/sewage; transmission: waterborne; portal: digestive mucosa
Reservoir: the river; transmission: biological vector; portal: parenteral
Reservoir: humans; transmission: droplet within 1 m; portal: broken skin
Reservoir: a fomite; transmission: direct contact; portal: intact skin

questions.explanation: Ingested pathogens enter through digestive mucous membranes.

questions.prompt: An ICU has many patients on immunosuppressive drugs, many catheters, and several MRSA patients. Which statement best explains its HAI risk?

options.text: MRSA is a zoonosis carried into the ICU by animals
It has too few reservoirs for MRSA to spread between patients
Catheters there act only as portals of exit, not entry
It combines compromised hosts, invasive procedures, and reservoirs

questions.explanation: All three reasons for HAIs are present at once.

questions.prompt: Why would killing a pathogen's ability to adhere be a useful drug strategy even if the drug doesn't kill the microbe?

options.text: Non-adhered pathogens convert into harmless normal flora
Adherence is required for the pathogen's portal of exit
Non-adhered pathogens get flushed out by urine, mucus, and coughing
Adherence is the step where pathogens manufacture their toxins

questions.explanation: Without adherence, the body's flushing mechanisms remove the pathogen.

questions.prompt: A diabetic patient develops dying, blackened foot tissue. Which enzymes and organism best explain it?

options.text: Coagulase from Staphylococcus aureus walling off the foot
IgA protease from Streptococcus pneumoniae in the blood
Collagenase and hyaluronidase from Clostridium perfringens
Kinase from Streptococcus pyogenes dissolving foot clots

questions.explanation: Breaking down connective tissue, including vessels, leads to gangrene.

questions.prompt: Which observation would best support Roux's hypothesis that diphtheria causes body-wide effects through a toxin?

options.text: A cell-free filtrate of an older culture alone causes the disease's effects
Unfiltered culture causes only a local throat infection in guinea pigs
Guinea pigs survive very large injections of fresh, 24-hour filtrate
Diphtheria bacteria are found spread throughout the patient's bloodstream

questions.explanation: If the filtrate (no cells) causes harm, a secreted substance is responsible.

questions.prompt: Why is the portal of exit medically important to know?

options.text: It determines whether the pathogen is Gram-positive or Gram-negative
It is the exact site where the pathogen's toxins are manufactured
It is always the skin, so skin care alone prevents all spread
It's usually the same as entry, which tells you how to block spread

questions.explanation: Once the pathogen exits, the host becomes a reservoir.

questions.prompt: Which virulence factor would be LEAST useful to a bacterium living inside host cells?

options.text: Invasins to get inside
Siderophores to grab iron
Ways to avoid antibodies in the blood
Fimbriae for sticking to the cell surface

questions.explanation: Once inside, fimbriae-based surface adherence is no longer needed — the cell can't be washed away.

questions.prompt: Lysogenic conversion links Module 15–16 (phages) to Module 19. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Lysogenic conversion produces the LPS endotoxin of Gram-negatives
Prophage genes can encode exotoxins that make a bacterium pathogenic
Prophages add an outer membrane that makes bacteria Gram-negative
Lysogenic conversion only occurs in fungi, not in bacteria

questions.explanation: Some toxins aren't encoded by the bacterium's original genes.

questions.prompt: A patient's throat infection stays local, yet he develops heart and nerve problems. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The infection is subclinical, so its effects appear elsewhere
An exotoxin from the bacteria travels through the blood (toxemia)
Bacteremia has spread the throat bacteria into every organ
Endotoxin is being actively secreted by the throat bacteria

questions.explanation: Like diphtheria: local bacteria, systemic toxin effects.

questions.prompt: Explain how capsules play roles in both adherence and avoiding host defenses, with an example of each.
questions.explanation: Adherence: the sticky carbohydrate capsule lets bacteria attach and form biofilms — S. mutans on teeth (and biofilms on catheters/contact lenses). Avoiding defenses: the capsule inhibits phagocytosis — encapsulated S. pneumoniae causes pneumonia while unencapsulated strains are fairly harmless.

questions.prompt: A patient has a catheter-associated UTI caused by MRSA. Trace the infection through reservoir, transmission, portal of entry, adherence, and avoiding defenses.
questions.explanation: Reservoir: another patient or colonized health-care worker (or the patient's own skin flora). Transmission: direct contact or indirect contact via equipment (fomite). Portal: the catheter bypasses defenses into the urinary tract mucous membrane. Adherence: biofilm on the catheter. Avoiding defenses: coagulase walls it off from white blood cells, and multidrug resistance makes it hard to treat.
